name: ogham

attributes.attribute: earliest form of writing in Irish
adapts Latin alphabet to twenty straight-line letters
letters divided into four groups of five sounds
twenty-first upturned arrow sign used for p in British inscriptions
each letter named after a tree (ailm for pine, beithe for birch)
letters for q, v, z support an Irish-through-Latin origin

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Ogham is the earliest Irish writing form. It adapts the Latin alphabet to twenty straight-line letters. Those letters are cut along the edge of a stone or wooden piece. The script divides into four sets of five sounds. A separate upturned-arrow sign serves for the consonant p in British examples. Notches and grooves are cut along either flank of a base line called the drum. Every letter takes a tree-name. Ailm for pine stands for the vowel a. Beithe for birch marks b. The presence of signs for q, v, and z, none of which Irish uses, points to a current view. The script carried Irish through the Latin alphabet. It did not grow from runic, Chalcidic Greek, or northern Etruscan sources. Inscriptions date chiefly from the fourth to the eighth century. They sit mostly on standing stones. Wood examples are known only by report. A 1945 survey counted 121 stones in Kerry and 81 in County Cork. Others lie across the island of Ireland and across Great Britain. The Isle of Man holds a few more. Five stand in Cornwall. Around thirty sit in Scotland, chiefly in Pictish areas. Over forty stand in Wales. South Wales took many settlers from southern Ireland, including the Déisi. Ogham also served Pictish. Welsh stones sometimes carry Irish ogham next to Brythonic-Latin lines. Druids treated sacred lore as too holy for written notes. They kept most teaching by memory. So few ogham stones survive and most record a single name. Surviving stones gather chiefly in Munster, with others in Wales and Britain.

okr.objective: Define ogham as the earliest Irish script, an adaptation of the Latin alphabet in twenty straight-line letters, and locate its surviving stones across Ireland, Britain, and Wales.
key_results: Ogham adapts the Latin alphabet to twenty straight-line letters carved on the edge of a stone or wood.
A foundation line called the drum carries notches and grooves on either flank.
Each letter carries a tree-name such as ailm for pine and beithe for birch.
A twenty-first upturned arrow sign stands for p in British inscriptions.
Surviving ogham stones date chiefly from the fourth to the eighth century.
A 1945 survey counted 121 ogham stones in Kerry and 81 in County Cork.
Ogham stones also appear in the Isle of Man, five in Cornwall, around thirty in Scotland, and over forty in Wales.
Ogham was used for Pictish and appears beside Brythonic-Latin inscriptions in Wales.
Druids treated sacred lore as too holy to write, so most surviving stones carry only a single name.
Munster holds the greatest density of ogham stones within Ireland.
okr.evidence: MacKillop 2008, s.v. 'ogham'; Monaghan, Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore.
